title: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indicate true affinity within a group.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For animals, belonging to two most distinct lines of descent, may readily become adapted to similar conditions, and thus assume a close external resemblance; but such resemblances will not reveal—will rather tend to conceal their blood-relationship to their proper lines of descent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “Analogical or adaptive characters”. Scope: animals (and plants) of distinct lineages living under similar conditions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Convergent evolution has clear measurable predictions and can be evaluated independently of morphology. Broad cross-taxon coverage is incomplete, but many replicated clade-level tests are possible now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify distantly related lineages independently occupying similar environments and test for convergent external morphology, then compare morphology-based grouping with independent molecular phylogeny. Convergence plus reduced classification accuracy supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:

Environmental similarity and external resemblance require prespecified metrics.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: External similarity, habitat and phylogenetic distance are all measured variables, and molecular trees are independent of the external form being judged. Public trees, morphological matrices and plant trait data cover enough classic and systematic cases to accept or reject the pattern, with plants and invertebrates less evenly coded than vertebrates. The confounding issues are real and are the ordinary ones of comparative methods, not a barrier to a decision.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure external morphological similarity, ecological similarity and phylogenetic distance jointly, and test whether distant lineages in similar conditions converge in external form while remaining distant on an independent tree. The claim is confirmed if ecology predicts external resemblance after phylogeny is controlled, and refuted if external resemblance is explained by relatedness alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar climate is only a proxy for the 'similar conditions' that actually shaped the external parts.

Some apparent convergence is retained deep homology that a coarse ecological label misclassifies.

External form is coded differently in each matrix, so a global resemblance score has to be harmonized.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form, then among bird species from different orders, pairs sharing an ecological niche should be closer in external morphology than pairs with different niches; external morphology should predict ecological niche better than it predicts order (deep ancestry), yet within an order it should still predict family membership well above chance.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: AVONET1 (BirdLife taxonomy) species with complete values for 11 external measurements were log-transformed and z-scored (n = 10999). (a) For every between-order species pair the Euclidean distance was computed; the mean distance for pairs with identical trophic niche and primary lifestyle was compared with pairs differing in both, and the ratio was tested against 200 permutations of niche labels across species. (b) Leave-one-out 5-nearest-neighbour prediction from morphology was scored with Cohen's kappa for niche (trophic niche x lifestyle) and for order. (c) Within each order with >= 3 families and >= 30 species, family was predicted by LOO 5-NN with congeners excluded from the neighbour pool, and kappa recorded.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Using AVONET (Tobias et al. 2022) species-level external measurements (beak length culmen, beak length nares, beak width, beak depth, tarsus length, wing length, Kipp's distance, secondary1, hand-wing index, tail length, body mass; log-transformed and z-scored) and AVONET ecological categories (trophic niche, primary lifestyle, habitat), three clauses are tested. (a) Convergence: among all between-order species pairs, the mean standardized Euclidean morphological distance of pairs with identical niche (same trophic niche AND same primary lifestyle) is at least 10% smaller than that of pairs with different trophic niche AND different primary lifestyle, with a permutation p < 0.01 (niche labels shuffled among species, 200 permutations). (b) Concealment between groups: leave-one-out k-nearest-neighbour (k = 5) prediction from morphology yields a Cohen's kappa for ecological niche (trophic niche x primary lifestyle combination) that is higher than the kappa for taxonomic order. (c) Affinity within groups: among orders with >= 3 families and >= 30 species, leave-one-out k-NN prediction of family from morphology (congeners excluded from the neighbour pool) gives kappa > 0.3 in a majority of such orders. Verdict 'supports' if all three clauses pass; 'mixed' if one or two pass; 'refutes' if none passes.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Clause (a) fails if same-niche between-order pairs are not at least 10% closer in morphology than different-niche pairs, or the permutation p >= 0.01. Clause (b) fails if morphology predicts order with kappa >= that for niche. Clause (c) fails if kappa for family within order is <= 0.3 in half or more of the eligible orders. No clause passing refutes the claim; (a) failing alone already refutes the central convergence statement and is reported as 'mixed' only if (b) or (c) pass.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: ratio of mean morphological distance, same-niche / different-niche between-order species pairs

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: permutation p = 0.0050 (200 permutations); permutation ratios ranged 0.979-1.019

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'very distinct lines of descent' is read as different bird orders; 'similar conditions' as the same AVONET trophic niche and primary lifestyle; 'close external resemblance' as proximity in the space of AVONET external measurements (bill, wing, tail, tarsus, mass), which are exactly the adaptive external characters Darwin had in mind. 'Almost worthless for classification between groups' is read comparatively: external form carries more information about ecology than about ordinal membership. 'Can indicate true affinity within a group' is read as external form still predicting family within an order. Only birds are tested (the claim is stated for animals generally); taxonomy (BirdLife/AVONET orders and families) is used as the measure of relatedness, which is a modern phylogenetically informed classification but not a dated tree.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds (ELEData.zip, file TraitData/AVONET1_BirdLife.csv)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Birds only; Darwin's claim covers animals generally and plants by extension.

AVONET measurements are linear external dimensions and mass; 'close external resemblance' in Darwin's sense also covers colour, texture and overall habitus, which are not measured.

Ecological niche categories are coarse (10 trophic niches x 5 lifestyles) and were partly assigned with knowledge of morphology, which could inflate morphology-niche association.

Orders are used as 'very distinct lines of descent'; divergence times between orders vary widely and no dated tree was used.

k-NN kappa for order and for niche are not on identical footing (different class counts and class imbalance); kappa corrects for chance agreement but not fully for class structure.

Some AVONET trait values are inferred from congeners (Inference column); these were retained and slightly inflate within-genus similarity, which clause (c) mitigates by excluding congeners from the neighbour pool.
